source.title: Scaling Laws Beyond Backpropagation
source.authors: M. Filipovich; Alessandro Cappelli; Daniel Hesslow; Julien Launay

record.tranche_reason: Applies compute-frontier scaling-law fits to the new training setting of Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA), comparing it with backpropagation (BP).
record.gate_note: The study reports fitted compute-optimal training-loss frontiers and states that DFA never beats BP at a given compute budget. It reports training loss, not held-out loss, and keeps token count fixed; therefore these results do not test the held-out-loss, extrapolation, or parameter/token allocation versions. Individual points are plotted in Figure 3, but the text does not give their exact values.
record.test_reason: The paper fits L(C) = (Cc C)^αC to compute-optimal frontiers as a tool to compare DFA with backpropagation. It assumes the power-law form, as in Kaplan et al. It reports no fit quality, residuals or held-out extrapolation check, and makes no claim about whether the form holds. Its result concerns DFA's compute efficiency relative to BP, not any version of the scaling claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that DFA is never more compute-efficient than BP for causal decoder-only Transformers (57M–509M parameters), even under the optimistic C = 2ND assumption. DFA has both a worse offset and a worse exponent, so the gap widens with scale (scenario D). They caveat that novel DFA practices or simpler architectures might differ.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a compute-optimal power-law frontier fit similar to the cited scaling-law approach, but compares DFA and BP on causal decoder-only models and reports training loss after a single epoch over fixed 30B-token data, rather than testing held-out-loss scaling or parameter/token allocation laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted frontier differs by training method (BP, DFA, shallow baseline). The authors also state that their DFA implementation choices, including preprojector error and asymmetric residuals and nonlinearities, affected performance; they do not report a controlled sensitivity analysis for these choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Fitted compute-frontier exponents differ by training algorithm. BP has αC = -0.071, DFA -0.040, and the shallow (top-layer-only) baseline -0.019. The DFA gap to BP widens with scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alternative credit-assignment methods (DFA) yield worse compute-scaling exponents than backpropagation for causal decoder-only LMs.

fits_no_version.finding: DFA is never more compute-efficient than BP at any budget, even under the optimistic C = 2ND accounting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For the tested causal decoder-only language models and compute assumptions, DFA does not outperform BP in training loss at a fixed compute budget.

record.peer_reviewed: I Can’t Believe It’s Not Better Workshop, NeurIPS 2022
record.problems: The reported loss is training loss, not held-out loss. The tested model range is 57M to 509M parameters, which the paper describes as over an order of magnitude, and the runs use a single epoch over fixed 30B-token data. The authors did not fully explore learning-rate schedules and architectural hyperparameters. Uncertainty estimates are not reported.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3 shows individual model-scale points, but exact point values are not stated in the text and are not extracted here; the aggregate fitted frontiers and the authors' explicit comparisons are recorded instead.

untested.parts: The power-law form is assumed and fitted, not tested. There is no fit-quality evidence and no separate N or D scaling; the compute range is about 2–3 orders of magnitude.
Tokens are fixed at 30B; there is no N/D allocation analysis.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
DFA is an alternative training regime, but whether its loss follows a power law is not tested, only fitted.
No comparison of fitting, schedule, parameter-counting or data choices; no curve bending examined.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labelled V7 'supports' on the grounds that exponents differ across BP, DFA and shallow training. That conflates differences between learning algorithms (different systems) with V7's claim about setup and fitting choices producing disagreeing laws, so it is removed. Training loss is effectively held-out loss here because training is a single epoch, but that does not change the verdict: the power-law form is assumed, not tested. No uncertainty or fit diagnostics are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports training loss rather than held-out loss; it does not test loss scaling separately with parameters, tokens, and compute when the other factors are not bottlenecks.
It fits frontiers to its runs but does not test predictions from small runs against runs orders of magnitude larger.
Tokens are fixed at 30B; the study does not estimate how loss-minimising parameter and token counts grow with compute.
It does not compare architecture details at fixed parameter count.
It studies causal decoder-only language models trained on English data, not other modalities or the listed training regimes.
It reports language-model training loss, not downstream-task performance or its predictability.

The study reports different fitted compute-frontier exponents for BP, DFA, and a shallow baseline. It does not test sensitivity to parameter counting, data, fitting method, or schedule choices in a controlled comparison; it does not test compute-optimal parameter/token splits or curve bending.

rows.subject: BP runs (aggregate compute-optimal frontier)
rows.stage_stated: Causal language modeling; single epoch over 30B tokens
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to the compute-optimal frontier

conditions.value: 30B tokens of English CommonCrawl data filtered with CCNet

rows.measure: Best power-law fit of compute-optimal training-loss frontier (αC and Cc)
rows.note: Aggregate frontier fit across runs; the authors report fitting L(C) = (Cc C)^αC.
rows.check: This is a fitted frontier parameter used as a comparator. The study assumes the power-law form and reports no goodness of fit, so the row cannot show whether V1 holds. Training loss over about 2–3 orders of compute, with no fit diagnostics, does not test V1. Linking it to V7 is also wrong: the training algorithm is a different learning system, not a fitting or setup choice.
